analysis.one_liner: Permanently extends federal rules letting renters stay in foreclosed homes until leases end or 90 days pass.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently protect renters in foreclosed homes never left committee and died when the 115th Congress ended, despite 18 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law from 2009 gave renters a safety net when their building was foreclosed: the new owner had to honor existing leases and give month-to-month tenants at least 90 days' notice before eviction. That law expired at the end of 2014. This bill repealed the expiration date and permanently brought those protections back, so a tenant wouldn't lose their home just because a landlord missed mortgage payments.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters living in homes their landlords have lost to foreclosure. Under the bill, a new owner of a foreclosed property must let tenants with leases stay until the lease ends (or, for short-term leases or month-to-month tenants, at least 90 days), instead of being able to remove them almost immediately. This protects families with children in school, seniors, and anyone who could be displaced through no fault of their own.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act of 2009 as it stood on December 31, 2014, so foreclosing parties must honor bona fide leases and give month-to-month tenants at least 90 days' notice before eviction.
Repeals the 2014 sunset provision, making these protections permanent rather than temporary.
Any federal regulations issued under the 2009 law would be revived along with it.

analysis.who_pays: Investors, servicers, and landlords who buy foreclosed properties and profit from clearing them quickly would lose the ability to remove sitting tenants on short notice. Lenders pursuing foreclosure face a property that is harder to resell with tenants in place. The cost is borne by buyers of foreclosed homes, who would have to buy with tenants' rights attached.

drawbacks.text: Renters who want to leave early lose flexibility: a tenant on a lease could be locked into staying in a foreclosed building for months, and month-to-month tenants still get only 90 days, which may not be enough to find and move into new housing in tight markets.

Buyers of foreclosed properties — including lenders and small landlords — face lower resale value and less control over occupied units, which could discourage purchases of vacant-risk properties and slow the clearing of distressed housing in some markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary renters — not being evicted overnight from a home they pay rent for because someone else's mortgage defaulted — outweighs the cost to buyers of foreclosed properties, who take the property subject to existing tenants, a condition common in ordinary landlord-tenant law. The main design weakness is that it does nothing to help tenants who are on short-term or month-to-month arrangements beyond 90 days.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on February 7, 2017, joined by 17 other members including Reps. Waters, Maloney, Cummings, and Lewis.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The committee took no further action on the bill — no markup, no report, no floor vote — for the rest of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investors and servicers who buy foreclosed homes kept the ability to remove sitting tenants on short or immediate notice, since the 2009 protections stayed expired. Renters in foreclosed properties remained exposed to quick eviction for another two years.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 17 original cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill out, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-led Financial Services Committee never moved the bill, so the fight split along party lines without ever reaching a vote.

industries.industry: Investors and servicers buying foreclosed homes
industries.note: The bill would require them to buy foreclosed properties with sitting tenants attached and honor leases or give 90 days' notice, reducing their ability to flip or re-rent units quickly. Its death preserved their ability to clear tenants on short notice. Renters' interest in staying housed runs directly against these buyers' interest in fast turnover.

Foreclosing lenders would face occupied properties that are harder to sell with tenants in place. Their interest in converting properties to cash quickly works against the tenant's interest in keeping their home.
